Schaffhausen
shahf'how-zen
n. (the Swiss city and canton on the Rhine, reformed in 1529)
German, probably Schiffhausen, the boat-houses, from the Rhine portage above the falls where cargo had to be unloaded.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Schaffhausen stands on the right bank of the Rhine above the great falls, the one Swiss canton wholly north of the river, and in the sixteenth century it was a free imperial city dominated by the Benedictine abbey of All Saints. Sebastian Hofmeister, a native, brought the evangelical cause home from the Zurich disputations in 1523 and carried much of the town; the council wavered under pressure from the Catholic cantons and expelled him in 1525, and for four more years the city hung between. In 1529, in the wave that followed Bern, the council abolished the mass, removed the images, and dissolved the abbey, applying its revenues to the school and to the poor. Schaffhausen then subscribed the First Helvetic Confession of 1536 and the Second of 1566 and has been Reformed since. Its history is a useful corrective to any account of the Swiss Reformation as a sudden municipal decision: here it took six years, one expulsion and two reversals. “Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a canton as a small territory or clan constituting a distinct state, and an abbey as a monastery governed by an abbot.

expand to see more

CAN'TON, n. A small portion of territory constituting a distinct government, as in Switzerland.

AB'BEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, governed by an abbot or abbess.

RE'VENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property.

IM'PERIAL CITY, A free city of the Empire, subject to the emperor alone.

Modern Corruption

The Rhine city that took six years and two reversals to reform.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the tidy narrative: the Swiss Reformation presented as a series of clean council votes, city by city, as though a magistracy heard the arguments and decided. Schaffhausen expelled its reformer in 1525 and reformed without him in 1529, and in between it was pulled back and forth by its neighbours' threats and its abbey's money.

The principle to recover is that a city's standing is a moral thing and its safety is not in its walls: “By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted: but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked” (Pro 11:11). Isaiah states what a reformed commonwealth is promised and what it is to be called: “afterward thou shalt be called, The city of righteousness, the faithful city” (Isa 1:26).

Usage

"“A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14) — the Rhine city above the falls."

"“By the blessing of the upright the city is exalted” (Pro 11:11) — the council's decision of 1529."

"“We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1) — not the abbey's revenues."
